title: Ravens over Ur
sum: The family line runs from Reu to Abram, each father with a named wife and a dated birth. Around them the world goes bad again: Noah's descendants make war, eat blood, build walled cities, crown kings and sell slaves. They make idols, and cruel spirits sent by Prince Mastema push them on.

Mastema sends ravens to eat the seed in the fields, and Terah is named for the poverty they bring. Then the boy Abram, who at fourteen has already turned from idols and prays to the Creator, drives the ravens back seventy times in one day. A year later he teaches the woodworkers to build a seed box on the plow, so the birds never see the seed again.
readings: Read as an expansion of Genesis 11
Genesis 11:20–26 is a bare list of names and ages. Jubilees turns it into a story of decline that explains why God had to call one man out of the nations, and why that man was Abram.
Read as a story about evil spirits
The chapter names a cause behind the idols, wars and famines: Mastema and his spirits. Abram's first acts undo their work, by prayer and by wisdom.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church reads Kufale as Scripture, so Abram's youth here belongs to the sacred history of the fathers, read with the Orit (the books of Moses).
views.H: Read as a work of its own time, the chapter shows the book's method: gaps in Genesis are filled with stories that make the fathers models of law and wisdom, and the names are explained by Hebrew word play (Serug, Terah, as Charles 1902 explains them).
views.N: Joshua 24:2 and Acts 7:2–4 show that Jews of the New Testament age took an interest in Abram before God called him. The spirits behind idolatry fit Paul's words that pagan sacrifice is offered to demons (1 Corinthians 10:20).
views.J: The story of Abram's youth was told and retold by Jews: Charles 1902 gathers the rabbinic debate on the age at which Abraham knew God.
views.W: Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers can value the chapter as an early witness to how Jews read Genesis, while noting that Scripture itself tells nothing of Abram before God's call (Genesis 12:1).

deep.b: Jubilees seldom leaves a trace in the church fathers, but the ravens did. Charles 1902 quotes Jerome's Letter 78 to Fabiola, a commentary on Israel's camps in Numbers 33. At the camp called Terah (Numbers 33:27), Jerome remarks that Abraham's father has the same name, and that in an apocryphal book of Genesis he got it by driving off the ravens that were eating people's grain. So Jerome knew this story and its source, though in his telling the hero is Terah, not Abram. A Syriac retelling under Ephrem's name and the history of Bar Hebraeus make the boy Abram the hero, as Jubilees does.

deep.title: Two answers to Mastema (Claude's reading)
deep.b: This is Claude's reading of the chapter's shape. Mastema attacks people at three points: their worship (idols, 11:4), their peace (war, 11:2) and their bread (ravens, 11:11). Abram answers two of them in this chapter, worship by prayer (11:17) and bread by a command and an invention (11:19–24), and the third in the next, when he burns the house of idols (12:12). The pattern matches Proverbs' picture of wisdom as a gift from God that feeds and protects (Proverbs 3:19–20; Proverbs 9:1–5).

echoes: Genesis 11:20–28; Joshua 24:2–3; Acts 7:2–4; Deuteronomy 18:10; 1 Corinthians 10:20; Numbers 33:27

settings.what: The angel's account of the generations before Abram
settings.when: during the forty days on the mountain (1:1–4)
settings.why: To show Moses how the nations fell into idolatry under Mastema's spirits, and how the young Abram turned from it, so that Israel's calling makes sense.
settings.readers: Jews of the 100s BC (the date on the book's audience card) who lived among nations that worshiped idols: the chapter traces the idols to spirits under Mastema (11:4-5) and shows the father of their nation turning from them as a boy (11:16-17).

title: Abram Burns the Idols
sum: Abram pleads with Terah to give up idols and worship the God of heaven who sends the rain. Terah agrees in his heart but fears the people. Abram marries Sarai, then one night burns the house of idols; his brother Haran dies trying to save them. The family moves to Haran.

There, on the first night of the seventh month, Abram watches the stars to learn the coming rains and realizes that all the signs are in the Lord's hand. He prays to be kept from evil spirits. God's call comes through the angel, who then opens Abram's mouth to Hebrew, the language of creation, lost since Babel. Abram copies his fathers' books, and Terah sends him to Canaan with a blessing.
readings: Read as a conversion story
Abram reasons his way out of idolatry and star-lore and chooses God before God calls him. The call of Genesis 12:1–3 becomes God's answer to a prayer.
Read as a story about language and learning
Hebrew returns to the earth with Abram, and with it the old books. The chapter claims that the knowledge Moses will receive was kept, in writing and in Hebrew, by a chosen line.

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox Church this is part of the history of the fathers in its Old Testament, and Abram's rejection of idols stands with Genesis's account of his faith.
views.H: Historians see the book's interests on display: idolatry, star-lore, the holy language and written tradition. Charles 1902 notes how the chapter protects Abram from blame, both for leaving his father (12:28–31) and in its treatment of Terah.
views.N: Stephen's speech (Acts 7:2–4) and Hebrews 11:8 tell Abram's call too. Abram's prayer to be kept from evil spirits sounds like the Lord's Prayer's "rescue us from the evil one" (Matthew 6:13).
views.J: Later Jewish legend has Abram thrown into Nimrod's furnace for refusing to worship; Charles 1902 shows that Jubilees knows only the burning of the idol house and Haran's death in it. The rabbis also told that God called Abram a prophet, not a star-gazer (Genesis Rabbah 44, as Charles cites it).
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as an early Jewish retelling. Its sermon against idols is close to the prophets, while its claims about Hebrew and the fathers' books go beyond anything the Bible says.

deep.b: Jubilees claims three things: that Hebrew was the language God used in creation, that it was lost to all humans when the tower fell (10:26), and that an angel restored it to Abram. George Syncellus quotes the claim from "the Little Genesis" in Greek, and Charles 1902 shows that the Christian Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions (1.30) also speaks of Hebrew as the language God gave the human race. A rival view, which Charles finds in Diodorus of Antioch, Augustine (City of God 16.11) and Cedrenus, held that Eber kept Hebrew because he took no part in building the tower. The Bible itself says only that the earth once had "one language" (Genesis 11:1) and never names it.

echoes: Genesis 11:28–32; Genesis 12:1–4; Joshua 24:2; Jeremiah 10:1–16; Isaiah 46:1–7; Acts 7:2–4; Hebrews 11:8; Galatians 3:8

settings.what: Abram's appeal to his father against idols
settings.when: in Ur, before Abram's marriage (12:9): in the year 1904 from creation by Charles's count, when Abram is 28 (born in 1876, 11:15). VanderKam's text gives no number for the year (see the variant at 12:1).
settings.why: To turn his father from idols to the God of heaven. For Moses and the book's readers it is a model sermon against idolatry, drawn from the prophets.
settings.readers: Readers living among idol-worshipers, who are given the father of their nation's own sermon against idols, and a father who agrees in his heart but keeps silent for fear of the people (12:7).

settings.what: Abram's prayer under the stars
settings.when: on the first night of the seventh month, in Haran
settings.why: To give up seeking the future in the stars and ask God to keep him and his offspring from evil spirits and show him the right road.
settings.readers: Readers who knew the Chaldeans' star-lore (11:8): the father of their nation gives up reading the rains from the sky and asks God himself (12:17-18).

settings.what: The call of Abram
settings.by: the Lord, through the angel of the presence
settings.when: the same night, in his seventy-fifth year
settings.why: To send him to the land and promise him a nation, blessing, and God as his God and his children's.

settings.what: Terah's blessing
settings.when: as Abram leaves Haran for Canaan
settings.why: To send his son away in peace, and to arrange for the family to follow him later.

title: The Land and the Tithe
sum: Abram travels through Canaan, building altars at Shechem and Bethel and offering burnt offerings. He sees a rich land and is promised it. A famine takes him to Egypt, where Pharaoh seizes Sarai and is struck with plagues; Abram returns wealthy. Lot parts from him and settles in Sodom, and God promises Abram the whole land and offspring past counting.

Four kings capture Lot. Abram arms his servants, and then the text breaks: VanderKam's text fills the gap with words in square brackets that tell of the victory and the tithe given to Melchizedek. The angel turns it into a law: a tenth of everything belongs to the Lord, for the priests, forever. Abram refuses the king of Sodom's plunder.
readings: Read alongside Genesis 12–14
Jubilees keeps the outline but changes the weight. It drops Abram's lie in Egypt and the herders' quarrel, adds offerings at every altar, and turns Abram's tithe into a law for all generations.
Read as law in story form
The chapter's center is not the battle but the tithe, "an ordinance forever." The fathers keep the law before it is given, so the law is older than Sinai.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads the chapter as part of its Old Testament; its law of the tithe stands beside the tithe laws of the Orit.
views.H: Scholars note the book's priestly interest: the tithe goes to "the priests who serve before him." The gap at 13:25 is a puzzle, since it falls exactly where Genesis tells of Melchizedek, the non-Israelite priest.
views.N: Hebrews 7 reads Abram's tithe to Melchizedek as proof of a priesthood greater than Levi's, the opposite use from Jubilees, which grounds the priests' tithe in the same gift.
views.J: The book speaks of a first tithe here and a second tithe in 32:10–11. Tobit 1:7–8 also knows more than one: a tenth for the Levites, a second tenth spent in Jerusalem, and a third-year gift for orphans, widows and converts.
views.W: Most churches read the tithe law as Jubilees' own teaching, not binding Scripture. Whether Christians must tithe is a separate debate, carded at Leviticus 27 and Malachi 3.

deep.b: In the manuscripts Charles used, the sentence about Abram arming his servants (Genesis 14:14) is followed at once by the middle of another: "... for Abram and for his seed, a tenth." Charles 1902 calls it an obvious lacuna. VanderKam's text, as transcribed for this site, prints words in square brackets that fill the gap: Abram killed Chedorlaomer, came back, tithed everything and gave it to Melchizedek. Genesis 14:15–20 tells of the rescue, the meeting with the king of Sodom and Melchizedek's blessing. The text as transcribed for this site does not show whether the bracketed words come from a manuscript or are the editor's restoration, so it is not certain how Jubilees told the story, or whether it named Melchizedek at all. The bracketed words also have Abram kill Chedorlaomer, where Genesis says only that he struck the kings and chased them (Genesis 14:15).

deep.title: Why might Melchizedek drop out? (Claude's theory)
deep.b: This is Claude's theory, not a finding. Two explanations are possible. A copyist's eye may have jumped from one word to a similar one, losing a few lines, which happens often in long texts. Or the loss may not be an accident: a book that ties every tithe to "the priests who serve before him" might be uneasy with a priest of God Most High outside Abram's line, whom later writers made a figure of great weight (Psalm 110:4; Hebrews 7; 11QMelchizedek). The manuscripts cannot decide between them, and the first is the simpler.

echoes: Genesis 12:4–14:24; Numbers 13:22; Numbers 18:21–26; Deuteronomy 14:22–27; Hebrews 7:1–10; Tobit 1:7

settings.what: Abram's first call on the Lord in Canaan
settings.when: on the first day of the first month, on the mountain of Bethel (13:5)
settings.why: To claim the Lord as his God ("You are my God, the eternal God") in the land to which he had been called (12:22).

settings.what: Abram's call on the Lord on his return from Egypt
settings.when: in the third year of the first week of the forty-first jubilee, at the same altar
settings.why: To give thanks with a burnt offering for his safe return, and to name God Most High as his God forever.

settings.what: The promise of the land and of countless offspring
settings.when: after Lot has parted from him, in the year of Lot's capture
settings.why: To comfort a childless man who has lost his nephew and to give him the whole land in promise.

settings.what: The law of the tithe
settings.when: told after Abram's tithe
settings.why: It binds Abram's offspring, every Israelite, to give a tenth of grain, wine, oil and herds, for the priests who serve before the Lord, forever. It answers the question of who supports the priests, and roots the answer in Abram himself.
settings.readers: Readers who supported the priests: the law gives the tithe to "the priests who serve before him" (13:25), not to the Levites as in Numbers 18:21-26, and roots it in Abram himself.

settings.what: Abram's oath to the king of Sodom
settings.when: after the rescue
settings.why: To refuse any wealth from Sodom, so that no one can say a king made Abram rich.

title: The Covenant Between the Pieces
sum: On the first of the third month God speaks to Abram in a dream: "I am your protector." Abram, childless, names Eliezer as his heir, but God shows him the stars: so will his offspring be. Abram trusts, and it is reckoned to him as righteousness. In the middle of the month he sacrifices a heifer, a goat, a sheep and two birds, guards the pieces from birds of prey, and in a trance hears of four hundred years of slavery and a return. A smoking oven and a flame pass between the pieces.

The angel says this covenant was made in the same month as Noah's covenant, the month of the Feast of Weeks, and that Abram renewed the feast. Then Sarai gives Hagar to Abram, and Ishmael is born in Abram's eighty-sixth year.
readings: Read as Genesis 15–16 retold
The chapter follows Genesis 15 almost line by line, with small changes from the Greek Bible, then jumps to the end of Genesis 16.
Read as a feast-day story
Jubilees dates the covenant to the Feast of Weeks and turns the rite into a sacrifice on an altar. The covenant becomes something Israel renews each year at that feast.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads this chapter as Scripture alongside Genesis 15; the verse of faith in 14:6 is one it shares with every church.
views.H: Scholars see the book's calendar argument at work: the great covenants fall on the Feast of Weeks, the fifteenth of the third month in the book's 364-day year (see 6:17 and chapter 15).
views.N: Genesis 15:6, copied here without comment, is the verse Paul uses in Romans 4 and Galatians 3, and James in James 2:23. The four hundred years appear in Acts 7:6 and Galatians 3:17.
views.J: Charles 1902 notes the rabbinic debates this chapter touches: whether there were one or three animals of each kind, and other chronologies that put the covenant on the night of Passover.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as a faithful retelling of Genesis 15 with additions; for them the verse of faith stands in Genesis, not here.

echoes: Genesis 15:1–21; Genesis 16:1–3; Genesis 16:15–16; Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6; James 2:23; Acts 7:6; Jeremiah 34:18

settings.what: God's promise of an heir and the vision of the future
settings.to: Abram, in a dream near Hebron
settings.when: the third month, after the war of the kings
settings.why: To answer Abram's fear that a servant will be his heir, and to tell him what his offspring will suffer and gain.

settings.what: The covenant of the land
settings.when: the night of the sacrifice
settings.why: To bind God by oath to give the land from Egypt's river to the Euphrates to Abram's offspring.
settings.readers: Readers who kept the Feast of Weeks on the book's date: Charles 1902 (on 15:1) shows that the book keeps it on the fifteenth of the third month, a reckoning that differed from the Pharisees' about the beginning of the Christian era. The land covenant is dated to that month (14:20).

settings.what: Sarai's proposal
settings.when: after the covenant, while Sarai is still childless
settings.why: To gain offspring for Abram through her Egyptian slave woman Hagar. The angel tells it without blame, and goes straight on to Ishmael's birth (14:24).

title: The Eighth Day
sum: Abram keeps the feast of the firstfruits of the wheat with new grain and burnt offerings. God appears, renames him Abraham, renames Sarai Sarah, promises Isaac, and gives the law of circumcision. Abraham, Ishmael and all the men of his household are circumcised that day.

Then the angel speaks to Moses directly. The law of the eighth day is written on the heavenly tablets: not a day early, not a day late. The highest angels were created circumcised, and Israel is made holy to stand with them. Every nation has a spirit set over it to lead it astray, but Israel has God alone. Yet Israel will neglect this sign, some leaving their sons uncircumcised like the nations, and for that there will be no pardon.
readings: Read as Genesis 17 retold
Verses 3–24 follow Genesis 17 closely, often agreeing with the Greek Bible against the Hebrew ("on the eighth day" in 15:14; "I will bless him" in 15:16).
Read as a warning to the writer's own people
Verses 25–34 turn from story to sermon. Charles 1902 heard in them the crisis of the 170s BC, when some Jews hid their circumcision and Antiochus IV banned it (1 Maccabees 1:15, 48).

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which reads Kufale as Scripture, circumcises boys, and Charles 1902 reports that the Beta Israel of Ethiopia kept the strict eighth day that this chapter demands.
views.H: Charles 1902 read the chapter's insistence on the eighth day against the Hellenizing Jews of 1 Maccabees 1:15 and Antiochus IV's ban on circumcision (1 Maccabees 1:48, 60). The idea that nations are ruled by spirits draws on Deuteronomy 32:8 and is shared with Sirach 17:17 and Daniel 10.
views.N: The chapter shows the view Paul argued against: that circumcision marks who belongs to God (Romans 2:28–29; Galatians 5:2–6; Acts 15). Its picture of spirits ruling the nations helps explain Paul's "basic elements of the world" (Galatians 4:3).
views.J: Jubilees allows no other day; the Mishnah later allowed the ninth to the twelfth day in some cases (Shabbat 19:5, as Charles 1902 quotes it). Jews have always held circumcision to be the covenant sign of Genesis 17.
views.W: Most churches read Genesis 17 as fulfilled in Christ; they value this chapter as a strong witness to how much the sign meant to Jews before Christ, while rejecting its verdict on the uncircumcised.

deep.h: When is the Feast of Weeks?
deep.b: Leviticus 23:15–16 says to count seven Sabbaths "from the day after the Sabbath" when the first sheaf is waved, and keep the Feast of Weeks on the fiftieth day. But which Sabbath? Charles 1902 sets out the old answers. The Pharisees and later the rabbis took "Sabbath" to mean the first feast day of Unleavened Bread, so the count began on the 16th of the first month and the feast fell on the 6th of the third month (Sivan), whatever the weekday. Others, among them the Sadducee-like Boethusians and later the Karaites and Samaritans, took it as the weekly Sabbath. A third view counted from the day after the seventh day of Unleavened Bread; Charles found it in the Syriac version and among the Beta Israel of Ethiopia, and he argued that Jubilees, which keeps the feast on the 15th of the third month (15:1; 16:13; 44:4–5), follows it too. The quarrel was real: a group that kept a feast on a different day was, in its own eyes, the only one keeping it at all (compare 6:32–38).

Verses 31–32 give one of the clearest early statements of an idea found in several places in the Bible's world. In Deuteronomy 32:8 the Dead Sea Scroll 4QDeut-j ties the borders of the nations to "the sons of God," and most Septuagint manuscripts to "the angels of God" (the Masoretic Text has "the sons of Israel"; see the variant at Deuteronomy 32:8). Sirach 17:17 says that "For each nation he appointed a ruler, / but Israel is the Lord's share." Daniel names the princes of Persia and Greece and Michael as Israel's prince (Daniel 10:13; Daniel 10:20–21). Jubilees goes further than all of them in two ways: the spirits are set over the nations "to lead them astray," and Israel has no angel at all, only God. Charles 1902 also points to Paul's "basic elements" (Galatians 4:3, 9) and to the powers of 1 Corinthians 10:19–20.

echoes: Genesis 17:1–27; Leviticus 12:3; Deuteronomy 32:8–9; Sirach 17:17; Daniel 10:13–21; Romans 2:28–29; Romans 4:9–12; Galatians 4:3; Galatians 5:2–6; 1 Maccabees 1:15; 1 Maccabees 1:48

settings.what: The covenant of circumcision and the promise of Isaac
settings.when: on the feast of the firstfruits, in his old age
settings.why: To give the covenant a sign in the flesh, rename Abraham and Sarah, and promise a son through whom the covenant runs.

settings.what: The law of eighth-day circumcision
settings.to: Moses, to command the children of Israel (15:28)
settings.when: at Sinai, drawing a law from Abraham's story
settings.why: It binds every Israelite family with a son, wherever they live, to circumcise him on the eighth day exactly, forever. The problem it answers is Jews who delayed, shortened or skipped the rite; the reward is a place among God's holy ones, the penalty to be cut off.
views: Against the crisis of the 170s BC
Charles 1902 read the passage against the Hellenizing Jews of 1 Maccabees 1:15 and the ban on circumcision of 1 Maccabees 1:48, 60.
A permanent rule for any age
Read in the Ethiopian church and by Jewish readers, the law is the eighth-day rule of Genesis 17:12 and Leviticus 12:3, stated as strongly as possible.
settings.readers: Charles 1902 (on 15:14) read the law against Jews who, under Greek influence even before Antiochus IV, had hidden their circumcision (1 Maccabees 1:15), and against Antiochus's ban on the rite (1 Maccabees 1:48, 60; 2:46). The book's date is discussed on its audience card.

settings.what: The prophecy of Israel's neglect of circumcision
settings.when: at Sinai, foretelling the future
settings.why: To warn that some in Israel will leave the sign and become like the nations, and that this sin will not be pardoned.
settings.readers: Charles 1902 took the "prophecy" as the writer's own present: on 15:34 he says that the author "has forgotten his rôle as a prophet and dropped into that of the annalist." Read that way, the first readers lived among Jews who had left their sons uncircumcised.

title: Sodom and the First Feast of Booths
sum: The angels visit Abraham at Mamre and promise a son; Sarah laughs and denies it. That month the Lord burns Sodom, Gomorrah and Zeboiim for their impurity, a judgment that will fall on any place that acts like them. Lot is saved for Abraham's sake, but his sin with his daughters dooms his line. Abraham moves to the Well of the Oath, and Isaac is born on the feast of the firstfruits and circumcised on the eighth day.

The angels foretell Abraham's six other sons and say that only one son of Isaac will be the holy line, a kingdom and priesthood. In the seventh month Abraham builds booths, offers sacrifices and incense for seven days, and walks around the altar with palm fronds: the first Feast of Booths on earth, now a law for Israel forever.
readings: Read as Genesis 18–21 retold
Jubilees keeps the promise, Sodom, Lot and Isaac's birth, and leaves out Abraham's plea for Sodom (Genesis 18:16–33), the meal for the visitors and the episode with Abimelech (Genesis 20).
Read as the founding of a feast
Everything leads to the Feast of Booths. Abraham keeps it in joy for the promised son, and his way of keeping it becomes the pattern written on the heavenly tablets.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reads the chapter as Scripture with Genesis 18–21; the feast that Abraham keeps here is the Feast of Booths of the Orit.
views.H: Scholars see the book's aim of rooting every feast in the age of the fathers, and its sharp line between Israel and the nations (16:17–18, 25). Details such as wreaths and circling the altar may reflect the feast as kept in the writer's day.
views.N: Jesus, Peter and Jude use Sodom as the great warning (Luke 17:28–30; 2 Peter 2:6; Jude 7). John 7 sets Jesus at the Feast of Booths, and 1 Peter 2:9 gives the church the title "a royal priesthood, a holy nation" that Jubilees gives Israel.
views.J: The Mishnah (Sukkah 4:5) describes the circling of the altar at Booths, once a day and seven times on the seventh day; Jubilees has Abraham circle seven times daily. Charles 1902 notes the rabbis' other dates for Isaac's birth.
views.W: Most churches read the chapter as a Jewish retelling that teaches how much the feasts meant, while holding to Leviticus' own reason for Booths, the memory of the wilderness (Leviticus 23:43).

deep.b: Jubilees describes Abraham's feast in the language of the later law: seven days in the seventh month, booths, burnt offerings with a goat for sin, a peace offering, incense of seven spices, palm fronds and "the fruit of beautiful trees" (Leviticus 23:40). But his offerings are not those of Numbers 29: two bulls a day instead of thirteen down to seven, seven sheep instead of fourteen lambs. Charles 1902 compares the peace offering, seven each of rams, young goats, sheep and male goats, with Hezekiah's offering in 2 Chronicles 29:21: four kinds, seven of each, though not the same animals (Hezekiah's include bulls). The book does not copy the law; it shows the father keeping the feast faithfully before the law was written down, and the angels approving (16:28).

echoes: Genesis 18:1–15; Genesis 19:24–38; Genesis 20:1; Genesis 21:1–4; Genesis 21:31; Exodus 19:5–6; Leviticus 23:33–43; Numbers 29:12–38; Deuteronomy 16:13–15; Luke 17:28–30; Jude 7; 1 Peter 2:9

settings.what: The promise of Isaac at Mamre
settings.when: the first of the fourth month
settings.why: To announce the son and his name, already written on the heavenly tablets.

settings.what: The judgment of Sodom and of Lot's line
settings.when: told with the destruction of Sodom
settings.why: To make Sodom's fate a standing law for every place that copies its impurity, and to explain the doom of Lot's descendants.

settings.what: The angels' message about Abraham's offspring
settings.when: the seventh month, at the Well of the Oath
settings.why: To tell which of Abraham's descendants will be God's holy people and which will be counted with the nations.
settings.readers: Readers who called themselves Abraham's children: the angels say that only one line of Isaac's sons will be the holy offspring, and the rest will be counted with the nations (16:17-18).

settings.what: Abraham's blessing of his Creator at the first Feast of Booths
settings.when: during the seven days of the feast at the Well of the Oath
settings.why: To bless God, who made him, because he knew that from him would come "the plant of righteousness" and a holy offspring; he names the feast "the feast of the Lord."

settings.what: The law of the Feast of Booths
settings.when: told after Abraham's first feast
settings.why: It binds all Israel, every year, in the seventh month, to keep seven days of joy, live in booths, wear wreaths and carry branches and willows. It answers how and why the feast is kept: as Abraham kept it, by the heavenly tablets.
settings.readers: Readers who kept the Feast of Booths: the law gives the feast's booths, wreaths, branches and willows (16:30) a beginning in Abraham, before Moses.
